passages.t: The first basket, and ‘My father was a wandering Aramean’
passages.happening:
The laws that began in chapter 12 end with two acts of worship. The first is for the day Israel has settled in the land and gathered a harvest.

The farmer is to take some of the first of his produce, put it in a basket, and bring it to the place God chooses (verse 2). He says to the priest, “I declare today to the LORD your God that I have entered the land that the LORD swore to our fathers to give us” (verse 3). The priest sets the basket before the altar.

Then the farmer tells a story. “My father was a wandering Aramean, and he went down to Egypt few in number and lived there and became a great nation, mighty and numerous. But the Egyptians mistreated us and afflicted us, putting us to hard labor. So we called out to the LORD, the God of our fathers; and the LORD heard our voice and saw our affliction, toil, and oppression. Then the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm” (verses 5-8). “And He brought us to this place and gave us this land, a land flowing with milk and honey” (verse 9).

He ends: ‘And now, behold, I have brought the firstfruits of the land that You, O LORD, have given me’ (verse 10). He bows down. Then he, the Levite and the foreigner rejoice together in all the good God has given (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The firstfruits were the first ripe produce of the harvest, brought to God before the rest was used. To give the first was to say that the whole crop came from him.

In Israel the gift did not come alone. It came with words. The worshiper had to say out loud how he came to be standing there with a basket in his hands. Worship meant telling the story as well as bringing the gift.

The story is very short, and it is the whole Old Testament so far. It has a homeless ancestor, a small family that grew, slavery, a cry, a God who heard and saw, a rescue, and a land. Some scholars have seen in it one of Israel's oldest confessions of faith, though how old it is has been questioned.

‘A wandering Aramean’ is most often taken to mean Jacob. His mother came from Aram, he lived there for twenty years, and he went down to Egypt with his family. The Hebrew word translated ‘wandering’ can also mean perishing. Either sense fits Jacob, a man without a home and often in danger. It is a humble way for a nation to speak of its beginning. Israel did not begin as owners of the land. It began as migrants with nothing.

Watch the pronouns. The speaker starts with ‘my father’. Then he says ‘us’ and ‘we’, as though he had been mistreated in Egypt and had cried out himself. He was never in Egypt. He may have been born centuries later. He still says ‘us’. Then at the end he says ‘I’ and speaks of what he has brought. Each generation puts itself inside the story and then adds its own basket.

And the joy is shared. The Levite and the foreigner, who have no harvest of their own, are named as part of the feast.
passages.later:
Exodus tells the part of the story the farmer sums up in a line: “So God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (Exodus 2:24).

The book of Proverbs turns the practice into a rule of life: “Honor the LORD with your wealth and with the firstfruits of all your harvest” (Proverbs 3:9).

Paul uses the picture of the first basket for the resurrection of Jesus: “But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). The first of a harvest is the promise that the rest will follow.
passages.asks: The farmer could not hand over his gift without saying where he came from and who brought him out. Ask whether you could tell your own story in five sentences: where you began, what you cried out about, and what God did. And ask what you bring to God first, before the rest of what you have is spent.

passages.t: The tithe for the poor, and a prayer
passages.happening:
The second act is for the third year, ‘the year of the tithe’. The tenth of that year's produce is given to ‘the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow, that they may eat and be filled within your gates’ (verse 12).

When it is done, the farmer makes a declaration before God. “I have removed from my house the sacred portion and have given it to the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow, according to all the commandments You have given me” (verse 13). He says he has not eaten any of it while in mourning, or handled it while unclean, or offered any of it for the dead (verse 14).

Then he prays. “Look down from Your holy habitation, from heaven, and bless Your people Israel and the land You have given us” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
The third-year tithe was described in chapter 14. It stayed in the local town and fed those who had no land.

Here the giver has to stand before God afterward and say that he has done it. There was no inspector. The tithe was given out in a man's own village, and no one else could know whether he had kept some back. The law makes him answer to God for it, out loud.

He calls the tithe ‘the sacred portion’. Food set aside for widows and orphans is called holy, in the same way as what is brought to the altar.

Three things are denied in verse 14. They have to do with customs around death. In the ancient world food was commonly set out for dead ancestors. Israel's gifts were for the living poor.

The declaration ends in a prayer and not in a demand. Having done his part, the farmer does not present a bill. He asks God to look down and bless. And he asks it for the whole people and the whole land. He does not ask for himself alone.
passages.later:
The psalms have prayers like the farmer's declaration, in which a worshiper tells God plainly that he has kept faith (Psalm 26).

Jesus told of a man whose prayer sounds a little like verse 14 and is its opposite. “God, I thank You that I am not like the other men”, he began, and he listed his tithes (Luke 18:11-12). The farmer of Deuteronomy looks at the poor he has fed and prays for his people. The man in the parable looks at his neighbor and despises him.
passages.hard:
Is it not proud for the worshiper to say, ‘I have done everything You commanded me’?

It can sound like a boast, especially to readers who know the New Testament's warnings against trusting in one's own goodness.

In its place the declaration is narrow. The worshiper is speaking about one thing, the tithe. He says that he has given it to the poor and has not misused it. It is the kind of statement an honest steward makes about a task he was given. It is not a claim to be without sin.

It also comes after a confession that everything Israel has is God's gift (verses 5-10), and it ends in a prayer for blessing. Readers of many traditions have noted that Old Testament faith holds together humble dependence on God's grace and sincere obedience in particular things.

The danger Jesus exposes in his parable is obedience that has turned into contempt for other people. That is the opposite of this chapter, in which obedience means that the poor have eaten and are full.
passages.asks: The farmer had to tell God that the share belonging to the poor had left his house. Ask whether you could say that honestly today. And notice how his prayer ends. Ask whether your prayers after you have done right are thanks and requests for others, or a quiet claim to be owed something.

passages.happening:
Moses closes the whole body of law with a few solemn sentences.

“The LORD your God commands you this day to follow these statutes and ordinances. You must be careful to follow them with all your heart and with all your soul” (verse 16).

Then two statements, set side by side. “Today you have proclaimed that the LORD is your God and that you will walk in His ways” (verse 17). “And today the LORD has proclaimed that you are His people and treasured possession as He promised” (verse 18).

God will set Israel ‘high in praise and name and honor above all the nations He has made’, and it will be ‘a holy people to the LORD your God’ (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
These verses are the seal on chapters 12 to 26. All the laws about worship, courts, kings, war, family and the poor are gathered up in one moment.

The two declarations mirror each other, in the way that the two sides of a covenant would each state their commitment. Israel declares that the LORD is its God. God declares that Israel is his people. It is the language of a bond between two parties who have chosen each other. The word ‘today’ stands at the head of both.

Israel's side has duties in it: to walk in his ways, to keep his commands, to listen to his voice. God's side has a gift in it: Israel is his ‘treasured possession’. The Hebrew word, used also in chapter 7, means a king's personal treasure, kept apart from his other wealth.

The phrase ‘with all your heart and with all your soul’ comes straight from the Shema in chapter 6. The laws were never meant to be kept as bare rules. They are the shape that love takes.

The promise of honor ‘above all the nations’ must be read with the rest of the book. Israel was chosen out of love and for a purpose, and chapter 9 has told it plainly that it is no better than others. What sets it high is to be a holy people, which means a people that belongs to God and shows what he is like. The laws just given describe that: honest scales, wages paid on time, and a field left for the poor. Nothing in the verse gives any nation of today a claim to stand above others.
passages.later:
God had first used these words at Sinai: “you will be My treasured possession out of all the nations” (Exodus 19:5).

The prophets carried the two declarations forward as a promise: “And I will be their God, and they will be My people” (Jeremiah 31:33).

Peter takes up the language for those who belong to Christ: ‘a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession’ (1 Peter 2:9). The note on 1 Peter 2 sets out how Christians understand that in relation to Israel.
passages.asks: The covenant is two declarations, one from each side. Ask whether you have ever told God plainly, in your own words, that he is your God. And ask whether you believe what he says in return: that he looks at his people as a treasure he has chosen to keep.
